nameStory: These tiny clams get their name from their resemblance to a fingernail - they're small, oval, and have the same translucent quality as a human nail. The 'swamp' part of their name hints at their preferred muddy, slow-water habitats where they filter-feed among the muck.
description: Swamp fingernailclams are tiny freshwater mollusks that look like miniature versions of ocean clams. These little filter-feeders have two hinged shells that are typically yellowish to brown in color and translucent enough that you can sometimes see through them. They rarely grow larger than a pea - usually just 3-8 millimeters long - making them easy to overlook in their muddy homes.

idTips.label: Shell size and shape
idTips.description: Oval shells about the size of your pinky fingernail (3-8mm), with a smooth, rounded outline that feels delicate when handled gently

idTips.label: Shell color and texture
idTips.description: Yellowish-brown to light brown shells that are translucent and smooth to the touch, often with visible growth rings like tree rings

idTips.label: Shell thickness
idTips.description: Notably thin shells that feel fragile and lightweight - much thinner than a marine clam of similar size

idTips.label: Hinge area
idTips.description: Small, simple hinge connecting the two shell halves, visible as a slight thickening along one edge

idTips.label: Interior appearance
idTips.description: Pearly white interior surface that feels smooth when empty shells are found

habitat: Look for swamp fingernailclams in slow-moving or still freshwater areas throughout New England - ponds, marshes, swamps, and sluggish streams with muddy or sandy bottoms. They prefer areas with organic matter and vegetation where they can filter microscopic food particles from the water. You'll often find their empty shells washed up along muddy shorelines after storms or during low water periods.

seasonality.spring: Active period begins as water warms; look for live clams moving slowly through shallow, muddy areas near vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when clams are most active and easiest to spot; empty shells often wash ashore during summer storms.
seasonality.fall: Still active in warmer areas; this is often the best time to find empty shells along receding shorelines as water levels drop.
seasonality.winter: Clams burrow deeper into sediment and become inactive; mainly dormant until spring warming begins.

funFact: These tiny clams are actually hermaphrodites that can reproduce by themselves, and the babies develop inside special pouches in the parent's gills before being released as miniature fully-formed clams - no larval stage needed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other fingernailclam species, but swamp fingernailclams tend to be more yellowish and are found in muddier, more stagnant waters than their pond and lake relatives. Remember: 'swampy and yellow' versus the clearer waters preferred by other fingernailclams.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they only live in swamps, these adaptable little clams can actually be found in many types of slow freshwater habitats - the name is somewhat misleading and reflects early collection sites rather than their full range of homes.
compareHints: Swamp fingernailclams are typically more yellowish than the pond fingernailclam and prefer muddier, more stagnant waters compared to the clearer habitats of lake fingernailclams. They're also generally smaller and more delicate than their lake-dwelling cousin, with thinner shells that break more easily when handled.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pond fingernailclams are typically smaller and more oval-shaped than their swamp fingernailclam cousins, which tend to be slightly more triangular and prefer marshier conditions.
Lake Fingernailclams are typically the roundest of the three Musculium species in New England, while Pond Fingernailclams tend to be more triangular and Swamp Fingernailclams are more elongated.
